input: Unplanned downtime continues to represent a significant operational challenge at the plant, where 180 pumps are currently in service. An analysis of maintenance records covering a period of 12 months reveals a total of 1249 h of unplanned downtime, with bearing failures accounting for 43% of the downtime hours. Against this backdrop, condition-monitoring sensors have been proposed as a potential means of detecting bearing deterioration at an earlier stage. A sensor set covering all 180 pumps has been quoted at $386k installed, plus an additional $58k per year. In a vendor trial conducted on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 25%, although it should be noted that this figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. It is also worth emphasising that spare-part lead times would remain unchanged by the sensors. On balance, it is recommended that a three-month pilot be undertaken on 24 pumps at a cost of $30k, with the reliability engineering group owning the pilot and reporting before the March capital review. The decision on full installation would be held until the pilot results are reported, ensuring that any larger commitment is based on evidence gathered at the plant itself rather than on vendor claims alone.
target:
Recommendation: run a three-month pilot of bearing-failure sensors on 24 pumps, at a cost of $30k, before any decision on full installation. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.

Maintenance records for 12 months show 1249 h of unplanned downtime across the 180 pumps at the plant, and bearing failures account for 43% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $386k installed, plus $58k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 25%. That figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, and the gap is what the pilot exists to close: a downtime reduction measured on the plant's own pumps under its own operating pattern. The sensors leave spare-part lead times unchanged, so any benefit the pilot finds comes through earlier detection of bearing failure, not through faster repair. The pilot is sized to the failure mode it has to detect: bearing failures dominate the downtime record, and the pilot pumps are drawn from the same population that produced the record, so a result on the pilot reads across to the fleet without a change of basis. If the pilot reproduces a reduction near the vendor figure, the case for full installation can be priced on plant data at the March review. If it does not, the expenditure stays at pilot scale, and the full decision is taken with the vendor claim still untested.
